title: Character Groups and Elementary LCA Duals

items.title: The multiplicative unit circle is a compact metrizable topological abelian group
items.statement: Let $\mathbb T:=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}$ carry the subspace topology of $\mathbb C$ and the multiplication of $\mathbb C$, and let $\varepsilon:\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\to\mathbb T$, $\varepsilon([t]):=\exp(2\pi i t)$, for the published one-dimensional torus $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$. Then $\mathbb T$ is a compact metrizable topological abelian group, $\varepsilon$ is an isomorphism of topological groups, and $|zw-z|=|w-1|$, $|z^{-1}-w^{-1}|=|z-w|$ for all $z,w\in\mathbb T$ with $|z|=1$.
items.strategy: The complex exponential is continuous on $\mathbb C$ and satisfies $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\,\exp w$, and it sends $t\mapsto\exp(2\pi i t)$ into the unit circle with kernel $\mathbb Z$ (cartesian form plus the zero sets of sine and cosine); the quotient universal property therefore induces a continuous bijection $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\to\mathbb T$, which is a homeomorphism because $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ is compact and $\mathbb T$ is Hausdorff. Multiplicativity makes it a group isomorphism. The unit circle is closed and bounded in $\mathbb C\cong\mathbb R^2$, hence compact metrizable by Heine-Borel; the two displayed identities follow from $|z|=|w|=1$ by expanding $|zw-z|=|z||w-1|$ and $|z^{-1}-w^{-1}|=|z-w|$.

references.title: Dikran D. Dikranjan, Introduction to Topological Groups (author lecture notes, Universita di Udine / Universidad Complutense de Madrid, 2007)

items.title: On a discrete domain the compact-open topology is the topology of pointwise convergence
items.statement:
Let $X$ be a discrete topological space ([[def-standard-topologies]]) and $Y$ a
topological space. Every compact subset of $X$ is finite
([[def-compact-space]]), and on $C(X,Y)$ the compact-open topology
([[def-compact-open-topology-for-topological-domains]]) coincides with the
topology of pointwise convergence ([[def-topology-of-pointwise-convergence]]);
hence on every $\mathcal F\subseteq C(X,Y)$ the compact-open subspace topology is
the subspace topology inherited from the product $Y^X$. In particular finite intersections of sets $\{f:f(x)\in V\}$, with $x\in X$ and $V\subseteq Y$ open, form a basis; these are open-coordinate constraints, not requirements that a coordinate equal a prescribed value.
items.strategy: A compact subset $K$ of a discrete space is covered by the open singletons, so it has a finite subcover. For finite $K$ the subbasic set $S(K,V)$ equals $\bigcap_{x\in K}\{f:f(x)\in V\}$, and the pointwise topology has exactly these sets as a subbasis; hence the two topologies agree.

references.title: Dikran D. Dikranjan, Introduction to Topological Groups (author lecture notes, Universita di Udine / Universidad Complutense de Madrid, 2007)
Manfred Einsiedler and Thomas Ward, Ergodic Theory with a View Towards Number Theory, Appendix C, printed pp. 429-439 (course-hosted full text)

items.title: The unit-circle arc $\{z:|z-1|<1\}$ contains no nontrivial subgroup
items.statement: Let $\mathbb T$ be the multiplicative unit circle and $D:=\{z\in\mathbb T:|z-1|<1\}$. Every subgroup $H\le\mathbb T$ with $H\subseteq D$ is trivial; equivalently, for every $z\in\mathbb T$, $z\ne1$, some positive power $z^{n}$ lies outside $D$.
items.strategy: If $z\ne1$ satisfies $|z-1|<1$, write $z=\exp(2\pi i t)$ with $0<|t|<1/6$; replacing $z$ by $z^{-1}$ we may take $0<t<1/6$. For $n=\lceil 1/(3t)\rceil$ one gets $1/3\le nt<1/2$, hence $|z^{n}-1|=2|\sin(\pi n t)|\ge 2\sin(\pi/3)=\sqrt3>1$; thus $z^{n}\notin D$. Applying this to a nonidentity element of a subgroup contained in $D$ contradicts closure under powers.

references.title: Dikran D. Dikranjan, Introduction to Topological Groups (author lecture notes, Universita di Udine / Universidad Complutense de Madrid, 2007)
Lynn H. Loomis, Introduction to Abstract Harmonic Analysis, D. Van Nostrand 1953, Chapter VII, Sections 34-35, printed pp. 134-140

items.title: The Pontryagin dual with the compact-open topology
items.statement: For an abelian topological group $G$ written additively, a **character** is a continuous group homomorphism $\gamma:G\to\mathbb T$ into the multiplicative unit circle, and the **Pontryagin dual** is $\widehat G:=\operatorname{Hom}_{cts}(G,\mathbb T)$ with pointwise multiplication and the compact-open topology as a subspace of $C(G,\mathbb T)$ (subbasis $S(K,V)=\{\gamma:\gamma(K)\subseteq V\}$ for compact $K\subseteq G$ and open $V\subseteq\mathbb T$). The evaluation pairing is written $\langle x,\gamma\rangle:=\gamma(x)$. The dual is written multiplicatively; through the isomorphism $\varepsilon$ of [[lem-unit-circle-is-a-compact-metrizable-topological-group]] it is identified with the group of continuous homomorphisms into the published circle $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$.
items.strategy: Definition only; no proof obligation. Fixes the target circle, the multiplicative notation on the dual, and the compact-open subbasis used by every later item.

references.title: Dikran D. Dikranjan, Introduction to Topological Groups (author lecture notes, Universita di Udine / Universidad Complutense de Madrid, 2007)

items.title: The compact-open character group is a Hausdorff topological abelian group
items.statement: Let $G$ be an abelian topological group. With pointwise multiplication and inversion, $\widehat G$ is a Hausdorff topological abelian group. Explicitly, for $f,g\in\widehat G$, compact $K\subseteq G$ and $\varepsilon>0$, writing $B(z,r)$ for the Euclidean ball, $S(K,B(f,\varepsilon/2))\cdot S(K,B(g,\varepsilon/2))\subseteq S(K,B(fg,\varepsilon))$ and $S(K,B(f,\varepsilon))^{-1}\subseteq S(K,B(f^{-1},\varepsilon))$.
items.strategy: Products and inverses of characters are characters because products of continuous maps are continuous and the target is abelian; the group axioms are inherited pointwise. For the displayed inclusions use $|f(x)|=|g(x)|=1$: $|f'(x)g'(x)-f(x)g(x)|\le|g'(x)-g(x)|+|f'(x)-f(x)|$ and $|g'(x)^{-1}-g(x)^{-1}|=|g'(x)-g(x)|$. Hausdorffness: if $f\ne g$, choose $x$ with $f(x)\ne g(x)$ and disjoint open $V,W$ in the metric space $\mathbb T$; then $S(\{x\},V)$ and $S(\{x\},W)$ are disjoint compact-open neighbourhoods. No choice principle is used.

references.title: Dikran D. Dikranjan, Introduction to Topological Groups (author lecture notes, Universita di Udine / Universidad Complutense de Madrid, 2007)
Lynn H. Loomis, Introduction to Abstract Harmonic Analysis, D. Van Nostrand 1953, Chapter VII, Sections 34-35, printed pp. 134-140
Manfred Einsiedler and Thomas Ward, Ergodic Theory with a View Towards Number Theory, Appendix C, printed pp. 429-439 (course-hosted full text)

items.title: Evaluation of characters is jointly continuous
items.statement: Let $G$ be a locally compact Hausdorff abelian group. The evaluation pairing $\widehat G\times G\to\mathbb T$, $(\gamma,x)\mapsto\gamma(x)$, is continuous for the compact-open topology on $\widehat G$ and the given topology on $G$.
items.strategy: Fix $(\gamma_0,x_0)$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Choose a compact neighbourhood $K$ of $x_0$ (local compactness), so that $K-x_0$ is a compact neighbourhood of $0$. For $x\in K$ and $\gamma$ in the open set $S(\{x_0\},B(\gamma_0(x_0),\varepsilon/2))\cap S(K-x_0,B(1,\varepsilon/2))$ one has $\gamma(x)=\gamma(x_0)\gamma(x-x_0)$ and hence $|\gamma(x)-\gamma_0(x_0)|\le|\gamma(x_0)-\gamma_0(x_0)|+|\gamma(x-x_0)-1|<\varepsilon$, using $|\gamma(x_0)|=1$.

references.title: Lynn H. Loomis, Introduction to Abstract Harmonic Analysis, D. Van Nostrand 1953, Chapter VII, Sections 34-35, printed pp. 134-140

items.title: Pointwise limits of characters are characters
items.statement:
(1) A pointwise limit of group homomorphisms $G\to\mathbb T$ is a homomorphism;
precisely, $\operatorname{Hom}(G,\mathbb T)$ is closed in $\mathbb T^{G}$ for
the topology of pointwise convergence
([[def-topology-of-pointwise-convergence]],
[[def-product-topology]]). (2) If a pointwise limit of continuous homomorphisms
is taken along an equicontinuous family, then the limit is continuous, hence a
character. (3) If $G$ is discrete
([[def-standard-topologies]]), then
$\widehat G=\operatorname{Hom}(G,\mathbb T)$ is closed in $\mathbb T^{G}$ for
the product topology.
items.strategy: (1) Pass the identity $\gamma_j(x+y)=\gamma_j(x)\gamma_j(y)$ to the limit using continuity of multiplication in $\mathbb T$. (2) The pointwise closure of an equicontinuous family consists of continuous maps. (3) On a discrete group every map is continuous, so $\widehat G$ is the set of all homomorphisms, which is closed by (1) and the fact that a pointwise limit of maps in the closed set is already a homomorphism.

references.title: Dikran D. Dikranjan, Introduction to Topological Groups (author lecture notes, Universita di Udine / Universidad Complutense de Madrid, 2007)
Manfred Einsiedler and Thomas Ward, Ergodic Theory with a View Towards Number Theory, Appendix C, printed pp. 429-439 (course-hosted full text)

items.title: Dual homomorphisms: continuity, and the annihilator of a closed subgroup
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice (used only in part (b), through the compact-lift theorem for closed subgroup quotients). (a) If $\varphi:G\to H$ is a continuous homomorphism of abelian topological groups, the pullback $\widehat\varphi:\widehat H\to\widehat G$, $\widehat\varphi(\gamma):=\gamma\circ\varphi$, is a continuous group homomorphism. (b) If $H$ is a closed subgroup of a locally compact Hausdorff abelian group $G$ and $q:G\to G/H$ is the quotient homomorphism, then $\widehat q:\widehat{G/H}\to\widehat G$ is a topological group isomorphism onto the annihilator $H^\perp=\{\gamma\in\widehat G:\gamma(h)=1\ \text{for all}\ h\in H\}$, a closed subgroup of $\widehat G$. No stronger claim is made for pullbacks along non-proper maps.
items.strategy: (a) $\widehat\varphi^{-1}(S(K,V))=S(\varphi(K),V)$ is open, and the map is a homomorphism pointwise. (b) A character of $G/H$ pulls back to a character of $G$ trivial on $H$, and conversely a character trivial on $H$ descends by the quotient universal property; the inverse is continuous at the identity because every compact subset of $G/H$ is contained in $q(K)$ for a compact $K\subseteq G$ (compact lifts of closed subgroup quotients), and $\gamma\in S(K,V)$ then gives $\widehat q^{-1}(\gamma)\in S(L,V)$; continuity at the identity suffices for a group homomorphism. $H^\perp$ is closed because it is an intersection of the closed conditions $\gamma\mapsto\gamma(h)=1$.

references.title: Lynn H. Loomis, Introduction to Abstract Harmonic Analysis, D. Van Nostrand 1953, Chapter VII, Sections 34-35, printed pp. 134-140
Dikran D. Dikranjan, Introduction to Topological Groups (author lecture notes, Universita di Udine / Universidad Complutense de Madrid, 2007)

items.title: Continuous characters of the real line are exponentials
items.statement: Every continuous group homomorphism $\varphi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb T$ is $\varphi(t)=\exp(2\pi i\xi t)$ for a unique $\xi\in\mathbb R$; conversely every such map is a continuous character of the additive line.
items.strategy: Compose $\varphi$ with the inverse of the isomorphism $\varepsilon:\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\to\mathbb T$ and lift the resulting map through the universal covering $p:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$; the lifting criterion applies because $\mathbb R$ is path-connected, locally path-connected and simply connected, so its fundamental group is trivial. This gives a continuous $\theta:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ with $\theta(0)=0$ and $\varphi(t)=\exp(2\pi i\theta(t))$. For fixed $t$ the continuous map $s\mapsto\theta(s+t)-\theta(s)-\theta(t)$ takes values in $\mathbb Z$, hence is constant, and it vanishes at $s=0$; so $\theta$ is additive and continuous, and the Cauchy-equation regularity theorem gives $\theta(t)=\xi t$ with $\xi=\theta(1)$. Uniqueness of $\xi$ and the converse are immediate.

references.title: Lynn H. Loomis, Introduction to Abstract Harmonic Analysis, D. Van Nostrand 1953, Chapter VII, Sections 34-35, printed pp. 134-140
Manfred Einsiedler and Thomas Ward, Ergodic Theory with a View Towards Number Theory, Appendix C, printed pp. 429-439 (course-hosted full text)

items.title: A compact identity neighbourhood in the dual
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $G$ be a locally
compact Hausdorff abelian group, $K\subseteq G$ a symmetric compact
neighbourhood of $0$, and $D:=\{z\in\mathbb T:|z-1|\le1/2\}$. Then
$N:=\{\gamma\in\widehat G:\gamma[K]\subseteq D\}$ is equicontinuous
([[def-equicontinuity-on-a-topological-domain-and-pointwise-relative-compactness]]),
is compact in the compact-open topology of $C(G,\mathbb T)$
([[def-compact-open-topology-for-topological-domains]]), and is a neighbourhood
of the identity character in $\widehat G$.
items.strategy: $N$ is a compact-open neighbourhood of $1$ since $1(K)=\{1\}\subseteq D$. Equicontinuity: given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $n$ with $\pi/\varepsilon+3\le n$ and put $U:=\{u\in G:ku\in K\ \text{for}\ |k|\le n\}$, a neighbourhood of $0$; if $u\in U$, $\gamma\in N$ and $|\gamma(u)-1|\ge\varepsilon$, then a representative $t$ of the argument of $\gamma(u)$ satisfies $|t|\ge\varepsilon/(2\pi)$, and some $k\le n$ has $kt\in[1/2,2/3]$ modulo sign, so $|\gamma(ku)-1|\ge\sqrt3>1/2$, contradicting $ku\in K$; translate by $x_0$ for equicontinuity at $x_0$. Closedness: if $\gamma_j\in N$ converge pointwise to $\gamma$, then $\gamma$ is a character (the family is equicontinuous, and pointwise limits of homomorphisms are homomorphisms) with $\gamma(K)\subseteq D$ since $D$ is closed. Ascoli's sufficiency theorem (Choice) makes the compact-open closure of $N$ compact, and closedness identifies it with $N$.

references.title: Dikran D. Dikranjan, Introduction to Topological Groups (author lecture notes, Universita di Udine / Universidad Complutense de Madrid, 2007)
Lynn H. Loomis, Introduction to Abstract Harmonic Analysis, D. Van Nostrand 1953, Chapter VII, Sections 34-35, printed pp. 134-140

items.title: The dual of a locally compact abelian group is locally compact abelian
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. If $G$ is a locally compact Hausdorff abelian group, then $\widehat G$ is a locally compact Hausdorff abelian topological group, and the sets $\{\gamma:\gamma(K)\subseteq V\}$ with $K\subseteq G$ compact and $V\subseteq\mathbb T$ open form a basis of neighbourhoods of the identity character.
items.strategy: The compact neighbourhood $N$ of [[lem-dual-identity-neighbourhood-is-compact]] gives local compactness at the identity; translations by characters are homeomorphisms of the topological group $\widehat G$, so every point has a compact neighbourhood. Hausdorffness and the topological-group axioms are [[lem-compact-open-character-group-operations-are-continuous]], and the stated sets are the defining compact-open subbasis around the identity.

references.title: Manfred Einsiedler and Thomas Ward, Ergodic Theory with a View Towards Number Theory, Appendix C, printed pp. 429-439 (course-hosted full text)
Dikran D. Dikranjan, Introduction to Topological Groups (author lecture notes, Universita di Udine / Universidad Complutense de Madrid, 2007)
Lynn H. Loomis, Introduction to Abstract Harmonic Analysis, D. Van Nostrand 1953, Chapter VII, Sections 34-35, printed pp. 134-140

items.title: Compact groups have discrete duals and discrete groups have compact duals
items.statement:
(1) If $G$ is a compact abelian topological group, then $\widehat G$ is discrete.
(2) If $G$ is a discrete abelian group, then, assuming the Axiom of Choice
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) used only through Tychonoff's theorem, $\widehat G$ is
compact ([[def-compact-space]]).
items.strategy: (1) For $G$ compact the set $S(G,D)$ with $D=\{z:|z-1|<1\}$ is an open neighbourhood of the identity in $\widehat G$; if $\gamma(G)\subseteq D$ then the image subgroup $\gamma(G)$ lies in the arc $D$, so it is trivial by the arc lemma and $\gamma=1$. Thus $\{1\}$ is open, and translations (the dual is a topological group) make every point open. (2) For $G$ discrete the compact-open topology on $\widehat G$ is the pointwise topology on the set of all homomorphisms $G\to\mathbb T$, a closed subset of the product $\mathbb T^G$ by the pointwise-limit lemma; Tychonoff's theorem (Choice) makes $\mathbb T^G$ compact, so $\widehat G$ is compact.

references.title: Dikran D. Dikranjan, Introduction to Topological Groups (author lecture notes, Universita di Udine / Universidad Complutense de Madrid, 2007)
Manfred Einsiedler and Thomas Ward, Ergodic Theory with a View Towards Number Theory, Appendix C, printed pp. 429-439 (course-hosted full text)
Lynn H. Loomis, Introduction to Abstract Harmonic Analysis, D. Van Nostrand 1953, Chapter VII, Sections 34-35, printed pp. 134-140

items.title: Duals of finite products and of discrete direct sums
items.statement:
(1) For locally compact Hausdorff abelian groups $G_{1},\dots,G_{n}$ the map
$$\Phi:\widehat{G_{1}}\times\cdots\times\widehat{G_{n}}\to\widehat{G_{1}\times\cdots\times G_{n}},\qquad \Phi(\gamma_{1},\dots,\gamma_{n})\big((x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\big):=\prod_{j}\gamma_{j}(x_{j}),$$
is an isomorphism of topological groups for the product topologies (choice-free,
finite $n$). (2) If $(G_{i})_{i\in I}$ is a family of discrete abelian groups and
$G=\bigoplus_{i}G_{i}$ is their algebraic direct sum equipped with the discrete
topology ([[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]), then, assuming the Axiom
of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), $\widehat G$ is topologically isomorphic to
the product $\prod_{i}\widehat{G_{i}}$ with the product topology. No claim is
made here about a direct sum carrying the subspace topology of the product of
non-discrete factors.
items.strategy: (1) The displayed map is a bijective homomorphism (restrict a character to the coordinate axes for the inverse). Continuity at the identity: for compact $K\subseteq G_1\times G_2$ the projections $K_j$ are compact, and $\Phi(S(K_1,V)\times S(K_2,V))\subseteq S(K,V\cdot V)$ for every neighbourhood $V$ of $1$; openness: for a compact $K=(K_1\cup\{0\})\times(K_2\cup\{0\})$ and $U=U_1\cap U_2$ one has $S(K,U)\subseteq\Phi(S(K_1,U_1)\times S(K_2,U_2))$. Iterate over $n$. (2) Restriction to the summands is a bijection onto the product of the duals; the compact-open topology on a discrete domain is coordinatewise convergence, and both sides are compact Hausdorff by the discreteness direction of [[thm-compact-groups-have-discrete-duals-and-discrete-groups-have-compact-duals]] and Tychonoff's theorem, so the continuous bijection is a homeomorphism.

references.title: Lynn H. Loomis, Introduction to Abstract Harmonic Analysis, D. Van Nostrand 1953, Chapter VII, Sections 34-35, printed pp. 134-140
Dikran D. Dikranjan, Introduction to Topological Groups (author lecture notes, Universita di Udine / Universidad Complutense de Madrid, 2007)

title: Character Groups and Elementary LCA Duals: Examples

items.title: The Pontryagin dual of $\mathbb Z$ is the circle
items.statement:
The dual of the discrete additive group $\mathbb Z$
([[def-integers]], [[def-standard-topologies]]) is canonically isomorphic to
the multiplicative unit circle ([[lem-unit-circle-is-a-compact-metrizable-topological-group]]):
the map $z\mapsto\gamma_{z}$ with $\gamma_{z}(n):=z^{n}$ is an isomorphism of
topological groups $\mathbb T\to\widehat{\mathbb Z}$. Under the identification
$\mathbb T\cong\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ this reads
$\widehat{\mathbb Z}\cong\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$.
items.strategy: A homomorphism $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb T$ is determined by $\gamma(1)$, and every $z\in\mathbb T$ defines one by $\gamma_z(n)=z^n$: the correspondence is a bijection and a group isomorphism. The domain is discrete, so the compact-open topology on the dual is the pointwise topology, i.e. the subspace topology from $\mathbb T^{\mathbb Z}$; $z\mapsto\gamma_z$ is continuous because each coordinate $z\mapsto z^n$ is, and its inverse $\gamma\mapsto\gamma(1)$ is an evaluation map, hence continuous. So the bijection is a homeomorphism.

references.title: Lynn H. Loomis, Introduction to Abstract Harmonic Analysis, D. Van Nostrand 1953, Chapter VII, Sections 34-35, printed pp. 134-140
Dikran D. Dikranjan, Introduction to Topological Groups (author lecture notes, Universita di Udine / Universidad Complutense de Madrid, 2007)
Manfred Einsiedler and Thomas Ward, Ergodic Theory with a View Towards Number Theory, Appendix C, printed pp. 429-439 (course-hosted full text)

items.title: The Pontryagin dual of the circle is $\mathbb Z$
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Every
continuous group homomorphism $\chi:\mathbb T\to\mathbb T$ is
$\chi(z)=z^{n}$ for a unique $n\in\mathbb Z$; consequently
$n\mapsto(z\mapsto z^{n})$ is an isomorphism of topological groups
$\mathbb Z\to\widehat{\mathbb T}$ (equivalently, the dual of the published
circle $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ is $\mathbb Z$).
items.strategy: Transport $\chi$ along the isomorphism $\varepsilon:\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\to\mathbb T$ to a character $f$ of the probability space $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$; continuity on the compact circle gives $f\in L^2$, and the published measure/Fourier theory is used under the stated countable choice. For the Fourier coefficients, substituting $x=y+h$ and using translation invariance of the Haar integral gives $\widehat f(k)=f(h)e^{-2\pi ikh}\widehat f(k)$ for every $h$; since $|f|=1$ some coefficient is nonzero (otherwise the expansion of $f$ in the complete orthonormal system $(e_k)$ would give $f=0$), so $f(h)=e^{2\pi ikh}$ for that $k$, that is $\chi(z)=z^k$. Distinct $k$ give distinct characters and every $z\mapsto z^k$ is a character. Both $\mathbb Z$ and the dual of the compact circle are discrete, so the bijective homomorphism is a homeomorphism.

references.title: Lynn H. Loomis, Introduction to Abstract Harmonic Analysis, D. Van Nostrand 1953, Chapter VII, Sections 34-35, printed pp. 134-140
Manfred Einsiedler and Thomas Ward, Ergodic Theory with a View Towards Number Theory, Appendix C, printed pp. 429-439 (course-hosted full text)
Dikran D. Dikranjan, Introduction to Topological Groups (author lecture notes, Universita di Udine / Universidad Complutense de Madrid, 2007)

items.title: The Pontryagin dual of Euclidean space is Euclidean space
items.statement: For $n\ge1$ every continuous group homomorphism $\varphi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb T$ is $\varphi(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,\xi\cdot x)$ for a unique $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$, and $\xi\mapsto\varphi_\xi$ is an isomorphism of topological groups $\mathbb R^n\to\widehat{\mathbb R^n}$.
items.strategy: For $n=1$ this is the classification of continuous characters of the line. In general $\varphi(x)=\prod_j\varphi(x_je_j)$ by multiplicativity, and each $t\mapsto\varphi(te_j)$ is a continuous character of $\mathbb R$, hence equals $\exp(2\pi i\xi_jt)$; this gives the stated form and uniqueness of $\xi$, since testing on coordinate lines and using $t\mapsto e^{2\pi i((\xi-\xi')_jt)}=1$ for all $t$ forces $\xi=\xi'$. Continuity of $\xi\mapsto\varphi_\xi$ follows from $|e^{2\pi i\xi\cdot x}-e^{2\pi i\xi'\cdot x}|\le2\pi\sup_{x\in K}|x|\,|\xi-\xi'|$ on compact $K$, and continuity of the inverse from the estimate $\sup_{x\in[0,1]^n}|\varphi_\eta(x)-1|=\sup_{0\le t\le\sum_j|\eta_j|}|e^{2\pi it}-1|\ge4\|\eta\|$ for $\sum_j|\eta_j|\le1/2$ on the fixed compact cube $[0,1]^n$.

references.title: Lynn H. Loomis, Introduction to Abstract Harmonic Analysis, D. Van Nostrand 1953, Chapter VII, Sections 34-35, printed pp. 134-140
Manfred Einsiedler and Thomas Ward, Ergodic Theory with a View Towards Number Theory, Appendix C, printed pp. 429-439 (course-hosted full text)
Dikran D. Dikranjan, Introduction to Topological Groups (author lecture notes, Universita di Udine / Universidad Complutense de Madrid, 2007)

items.title: The Pontryagin dual of a finite cyclic group
items.statement: For $N\ge1$ every continuous homomorphism $\chi:\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\to\mathbb T$ is $\chi([m])=\exp(2\pi i\,km/N)$ for a unique $k\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$, and $k\mapsto\chi_k$ is an isomorphism of topological groups $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\to\widehat{\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z}$ for the presented group; no generator of an abstract cyclic group is chosen.
items.strategy: A character of $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ is determined by $\zeta=\chi([1])$ with $\zeta^N=1$; writing $\zeta=\exp(2\pi it)$ and using that $\exp(2\pi iu)=1$ exactly for integers $u$, the roots of unity are exactly $\exp(2\pi ik/N)$, $k=0,\dots,N-1$. This gives a bijective homomorphism $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\to\widehat{\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z}$; the group $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ is compact, so its dual is discrete, and both sides are finite discrete, so the bijection is a homeomorphism.

references.title: Dikran D. Dikranjan, Introduction to Topological Groups (author lecture notes, Universita di Udine / Universidad Complutense de Madrid, 2007)
Manfred Einsiedler and Thomas Ward, Ergodic Theory with a View Towards Number Theory, Appendix C, printed pp. 429-439 (course-hosted full text)
